# Nasser Ghanemzadeh

> Independent forward deployed AI engineer for founder-led B2B SaaS. Sells the FDE Sprint: one working AI workflow shipped into your product in ten business days, fixed price, full refund if it doesn't ship. Building Vectig in public with Claude Code. Former CEO/CPO at Nivo (acquired, 200K+ users).

Nasser Ghanemzadeh has spent 17+ years building products and companies across AI, SaaS, and fintech. As CEO and CPO of Nivo, holding both roles at once, he built the product organization and shipped AI-powered applications that grew to 200K+ users and 450% revenue growth before the company was acquired. His current commercial focus is the FDE Sprint: a 10-business-day engagement for founder-led B2B SaaS teams of 5 to 50 that ships one narrow AI workflow into their product, with fixed scope, fixed price, and a full refund if there is no working prototype by Day 5 or no working workflow by Day 10. Founders start with the free two-minute AI Workflow Scorecard and a free 15-minute Scoping Call.

His live R&D lab is Vectig, an AI-native cash flow forecasting product for pre-seed-to-Series-A founders, built solo with Claude Code, in public. Most workflow patterns he ships into a client codebase have already run in Vectig first.

He is the author of three books: Daily Wisdom (366 one-page meditations on mental models, misjudgment, and money for founders, investors, and managers; out October 6, 2026 on Kindle, in paperback, and in hardcover), Forward Deployed AI Engineering (a working guide to the Forward Deployed AI Engineer role: what it is, where it came from, how it is practiced, and how to do it well; 304 pages, first edition May 2026, Version 1.5 August 2026) and Founder Mode (how great founders stay close to product, people, judgment, and execution as companies scale). He writes a weekly newsletter, Nasser Ghanemzadeh’s Newsletter, which runs one real decision through one mental model for founders who invest and investors who build, and his work has been covered in Forbes, TechCrunch, Al Jazeera, and HuffPost.

# AI Agency vs Forward Deployed Engineer: Which to Hire

URL: https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-agency-vs-forward-deployed-engineer/

[Forward Deployed Engineer](https://ghanemzadeh.com/forward-deployed-ai-engineer/)

## AI agency vs forward deployed engineer: which one ships your first AI feature?

An AI agency sells a team and a project: discovery, design, a build, a launch. A forward deployed engineer sells one senior engineer inside your codebase, shipping one AI workflow your own team will run. If you have no engineering team to own the result, hire the agency. If you have a product and a team, and you need AI working inside it, the forward deployed engineer is usually the faster route.

By [Nasser Ghanemzadeh](https://ghanemzadeh.com/). Last updated October 2026.

### What an AI agency sells

A team: a project or account manager, designers, engineers, sometimes a data scientist. The engagement usually starts with a paid discovery phase, produces a statement of work, and runs in sprints against it. Changes after that go through change orders.

That structure is the agency's strength when the job is big and you have nobody to do it. It is overhead when the job is one workflow inside a product that already exists. The people who scope the work are often not the people who build it, and the agency's best engineers are spread across several clients.

### What a forward deployed engineer sells

One senior engineer, working in your repository, on your data, with your team. The [forward deployed engineer](https://ghanemzadeh.com/forward-deployed-ai-engineer/) scopes the workflow with the person who will use it, builds it inside your product, evaluates it against real examples, and hands it over with what your engineers need to run it: the code, an output rubric, a playbook, and a walkthrough.

The same person scopes and builds, so nothing is lost between the sales call and the code. The limit is capacity: one engineer ships one narrow workflow at a time, not a whole product.

### Side by side

| Compared on | AI agency | Forward deployed engineer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who does the work | A team, with a management layer between you and the engineers | One senior engineer, working directly with you |
| Where the code lives | Sometimes the agency's stack or hosting, sometimes your repo | Your repository, from the first commit |
| How scope is set | Discovery phase, then a statement of work and change orders | One workflow, written as one sentence, agreed on the first day |
| Time to a first working version | Weeks to months, after discovery | Days, for one narrow workflow on your data |
| Who owns it after | Often the agency, through a retainer, unless the handoff is in the contract | Your team, with a rubric, playbook, and walkthrough |
| Best when | You need a whole product or several features built, and have no team to build them | You have a product and a team, and need one AI workflow live inside it |

### When the agency is the better choice

- **You have no engineering team.** Someone has to run and change the AI feature after it ships. If nobody on staff can, a forward deployed engineer's handoff has no one to hand to, and an agency retainer is the honest answer.

- **The job is a product, not a workflow.** A new app with design, mobile, backend, and AI all at once needs more hands than one engineer has.

- **You need work in parallel.** Three features on three deadlines need three builders.

- **Procurement needs a firm.** Some buyers require a company with insurance, security reviews, and a bench behind it.

### When the forward deployed engineer is the better choice

- **The product exists and the team is busy.** Your engineers can maintain an AI workflow; they don't have the weeks to learn to ship the first one.

- **The work is one narrow workflow.** One user, one input, one output, and a human check before anything leaves.

- **You want to own it.** Code in your repo, prompts and evaluation set in your repo, and no retainer to keep it running.

- **You want to learn before you hire.** One shipped workflow tells you what an AI engineer on staff would actually do, before you write the job description.

### Whichever you pick, put this in the contract

- The scope as one sentence: who uses it, what goes in, what comes out.

- Acceptance criteria, written before the build, that say what a correct output looks like.

- An evaluation set of real examples, so a prompt change can be tested instead of argued about.

- A handoff your team can run without the vendor: documentation, a rubric, and a recorded walkthrough.

- A data processing agreement with your model provider, such as Anthropic or OpenAI.

- Plain ownership: the code, prompts, and evaluation set are yours.

The [FDE Sprint](https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-feature-sprint/) is the fixed-scope version of the forward deployed route: one workflow, a working prototype on your data by Day 5, in your repo by Day 10, at a fixed price with a full refund if either milestone is missed. To compare it with hiring and contracting on cost, use the [FDE cost calculator](https://ghanemzadeh.com/fde-cost-calculator/).

### Frequently asked questions

#### Should I hire an AI agency or a forward deployed engineer?

Hire an agency when you need a team to build something you don't have an engineering team to own: a whole product, or design, mobile, and backend at once. Bring in a forward deployed engineer when you have a product and a team, and you need one AI workflow shipped inside your codebase that your engineers will run afterward.

#### Is a forward deployed engineer cheaper than an AI agency?

For a single, narrow workflow, usually, because there is one senior engineer instead of a team with a project management layer, and no long discovery phase. For a large build, compare the quotes on cost per shipped, accepted workflow rather than on day rates, and count the handoff: work your team can't maintain is not finished.

#### What should an AI development contract include?

One sentence of scope agreed before work starts, acceptance criteria that say what a correct output looks like, an evaluation set to test against, a handoff your team can run without the vendor, a data processing agreement with the model provider, and a clear statement that the code and prompts belong to you.

Not sure your workflow is narrow enough? Compare it with the [30 narrow AI workflows for B2B SaaS](https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-workflows-for-saas/), [score it](https://ghanemzadeh.com/scorecard/) in two minutes, then [book a 15-minute Scoping Call](https://ghanemzadeh.com/call/).

An AI workflow running in my own product, end to end, and how one gets built into yours. 16 minutes.

### What is the FDE Sprint?

The FDE Sprint is a fixed-scope engagement in which an independent forward deployed engineer ships one AI workflow into your product in ten business days. It's built for founder-led B2B SaaS teams of 5 to 50 people, and the workflow runs on your data. It's a fixed price, $5,000, refunded in full if there's no working prototype by Day 5 or no working workflow by Day 10.

### What is a forward deployed AI engineer?

A forward deployed AI engineer works inside the customer's codebase and ships AI features into their product, instead of advising from outside. The term comes from Palantir. In 2026, OpenAI and Anthropic both built teams around it to deploy their models inside customers. The FDE Sprint is the founder-tier version of that work.

Weighing a hire? [Does a startup need a forward deployed engineer?](https://ghanemzadeh.com/forward-deployed-engineer-for-startups/) compares a full-time hire, a contractor, and a Sprint.

As covered in

Forbes · TechCrunch · Al Jazeera · HuffPost

02 · The problem

### Your team knows AI matters. The hard part is shipping the right thing.

Most SaaS teams are already experimenting: someone has tried Claude Code, built a prototype, or floated a chatbot. The experiments stall because a useful AI feature needs more than a demo. It needs a clear workflow, the right data, a narrow scope, and an implementation path the team can actually ship.

That's what the Sprint produces: one managed AI workflow with a clear use case, a review process, and a handoff your team can run with.

03 · The model

### What is Forward Deployed AI Engineering?

Forward Deployed AI Engineering is a delivery model where an engineer embeds inside a customer's team and ships AI capabilities directly into the customer's product and codebase. The deliverable is working code in the customer's repo, not a deck about it. The term comes from Palantir, where it has been the dominant model for two decades. In May 2026, Anthropic announced a new AI services company with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs, in which its Applied AI engineers build Claude systems for mid-sized companies. Days later, OpenAI launched the OpenAI Deployment Company, with more than $4 billion of investment, to place Forward Deployed Engineers inside customer organizations. The **FDE Sprint is the same playbook, sized for founder-led B2B SaaS teams of 5 to 50 people** who can't run a quarter-million-dollar procurement process.

More on the role: [what a Forward Deployed AI Engineer is](https://ghanemzadeh.com/forward-deployed-ai-engineer/), and the full guide in the book, [Forward Deployed AI Engineering: The Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) Guide to Shipping Enterprise AI from Pilot to Production](https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/forward-deployed-ai-engineering/).

04 · Example workflows

### Examples of narrow AI workflows

- **Investor update assistant.** Reads the month's metrics from Stripe or your finance sheet, plus a few sentences from the founder, and drafts the update in your usual format. The founder edits and sends.

- **Runway scenario explainer.** Takes a proposed change (a hire, a price change, a churn assumption), runs it against current burn and revenue, and writes a plain-language note on what it does to runway. Someone checks the numbers before anyone acts on them.

- **Customer summary generator.** Pulls an account's CRM notes, usage events, and open tickets, and writes a one-page summary into the CRM record before a renewal call. The account owner reads it before the call.

- **Support ticket summarizer.** Reads a long Zendesk or Intercom thread and writes the issue, urgency, what has been tried, and a suggested next step into the ticket sidebar. The agent accepts it, edits it, or ignores it.

- **Report generator.** Turns a week of product data or notes into your weekly customer or internal report, in your template, as a draft. Whoever sends it reviews it first.

- **Onboarding assistant.** Uses a new account's setup data to suggest the next step in your product's first key workflow, inside the app. It suggests; the user clicks.

Thirty more, grouped by team, with the data each one needs and whether it fits a first Sprint: [AI use cases for B2B SaaS](https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-workflows-for-saas/).

05 · Proof

### A concrete example: Investor Update Assistant

Here's a workflow I've built into Vectig, the AI-native startup finance product I'm developing in parallel. The Investor Update Assistant pulls structured monthly metrics (MRR, burn, runway, hires, churn, key wins), takes 3–5 sentences of founder-written context, and generates a clean investor update draft. The founder edits, approves, and sends. In my own test runs, open to send took about 8 minutes, against the 90+ minutes a blank-page update usually takes.

What you'd get in a Sprint: the workflow scoped to your data sources (Stripe, your spreadsheet, your CRM, whatever you use), a working prompt with output quality rubric, integration into your existing product or admin tool, and the handoff document so your team can maintain and iterate. Two weeks. Live by Day 10.

### The numbers I can show you today

Every Sprint workflow ships with an output quality rubric, so each engagement produces its own before-and-after numbers. No Sprint has closed yet, and Vectig is still early, so the two rows below come from my own test runs of the Investor Update Assistant during development, not from customer usage.

| Metric | Before | After | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Investor update draft time, open to send | 90+ minutes of blank-page writing | 8 minutes | My test runs during development |
| Output quality rubric score | Not measured | 4-of-5 average across accuracy, clarity, honesty, and ask-coverage | 30 test runs during development |

The draft-time number measures the founder's full loop: open the workflow, review the generated draft, edit, and send. The rubric score is the average across the four dimensions the workflow is graded on, scored run by run.

As Sprints complete, their numbers land here.

### This is not an AI science project.

This is not:

- A generic AI strategy workshop

- A chatbot brainstorm

- A 40-page roadmap

- An attempt to make your whole product "AI-native" in two weeks

- A replacement for your engineering team

- A vague exploration of agents, copilots, and buzzwords

- A compliance-heavy enterprise AI transformation

The sprint is intentionally narrow: one workflow, one clear user problem, one useful shipped outcome.

06 · Day 0

### Day 0: the readiness check

Before a Sprint starts, we check your use case, data, codebase, and team. Below is what a typical founder-led SaaS team looks like at the start. The scorecard and the Scoping Call map these gaps, so the Sprint begins on Day 1 with them already known.

~/sprint-readiness/check.md

$ run readiness_check --target founder-saas

**use case**

vague

**data sources**

scattered

**codebase access**

ready

**AI provider setup**

configured

**team availability**

partial

**success criteria**

undefined

→ recommended path: 15-minute Scoping Call to pick the workflow and define success criteria.

Run yours: [Score your workflow](https://ghanemzadeh.com/scorecard/), two minutes.

Output simulated for a typical founder-led team.

### What the workflow is worth to you

The Sprint has a fixed price. What the workflow is worth depends on your numbers, so we work them out on the Scoping Call and write them into the Brief.

For an internal workflow the math is short: the hours a week the work takes today, times the loaded hourly cost of the people doing it, times 52. That's what the work costs you in a year. Divide the Sprint price by what the workflow saves each week, and you have the payback period.

**Worked example, with example inputs.** Four support agents each spend ten hours a week reading long ticket threads before they can reply. A summarizer that halves that saves 20 hours a week. At a loaded cost of $40 an hour, that's $800 a week, or $41,600 a year. The Sprint pays for itself in under ten weeks at either published price.

For a customer-facing feature, hours saved is the wrong measure. The value is in the deals the feature helps close or the accounts it helps keep, and the Brief names that metric instead. If neither number is bigger than the Sprint price, I'll say so on the call.

08 · How it works

### How the 10-business-day sprint works

**Day 1: Scope**

Define the workflow, user problem, available data, constraints, and success criteria.

**Days 2 to 3: Design**

Map the UX flow, architecture, prompt and data structure, and implementation plan.

**Days 4 to 5: Prototype**

Build the first working version and validate the direction.

**Days 6 to 9: Implementation**

Refine the workflow, handle edge cases, add error states, improve prompts, prepare for handoff or deployment.

**Day 10: Handoff**

Staging deployment, production-ready pull request, or implementation handoff, depending on your infrastructure and access.

### Why Day 1 decides the Sprint

I learned this on my own product first. The first AI features I built for Vectig were based on the wrong hypothesis: they solved a problem founders didn't actually have. It took conversations with founders, more research, and several pivots before the workflow pointed at something they really need.

Most stalled AI features go wrong the same way, before any code is written. So the Sprint starts by pinning the workflow down in one signed sentence, with the person who'll use it, and nothing gets built until that sentence holds.

### How a Sprint gets scoped on Day 1

Every Sprint Brief is written around a single sentence:

> *For [user], when [trigger or input] happens, the workflow will [process or action] and produce [output], so that [business value].*

**Worked example.** "For the founder, when monthly metrics and 3 to 5 sentences of context are added, the workflow will draft a clean investor update covering metrics, risks, and asks, so that the founder can send consistent updates in 8 minutes instead of 90."

Under the sentence goes one value line: the hours a week the work takes today, times the loaded hourly cost, times 52. For a customer-facing feature, it's the deal or retention metric the workflow moves.

**Value line for the example.** 82 minutes saved a month is not where the money is. The value is an update that goes out every month, on time, which keeps investors close before the next round.

If we can't agree on the words that fill those five brackets on Day 1, the Sprint isn't ready to start.

### The output quality rubric

Every Sprint ships with a 1 to 5 rubric tuned to its specific dimensions. The scale is fixed; the dimensions change per workflow.

| Score | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Unusable. Output is wrong, incoherent, or unsafe. |
| 2 | Needs major rewrite. Shape is right; substance requires substantial editing. |
| 3 | Usable with significant edits. Team starts from this draft but invests real time refining. |
| 4 | Good with minor edits. Small adjustments only. Usable in roughly the time it takes to read. |
| 5 | Ready to use. No edits needed. Ships as-is. |

Each workflow's rubric specifies its own dimensions: accuracy, clarity, tone, format, completeness. Each comes with worked examples at every score level.

### What we'll take on as a first Sprint

- Low risk Internal-only workflows. Drafts and summaries reviewed by a human before anything leaves the company. Most first Sprints sit here, and they should.

- Medium risk Workflows touching customer-facing data (support tickets, CRM notes, sales transcripts, internal financial data) with explicit human review.

- High risk Legal, medical, compliance, payments, or anything that takes customer-facing actions autonomously. Declined as a first Sprint. We'll help redefine to a lower-risk scope, or wait until trust and tooling are mature.

### Clear scope. Clear expectations.

The sprint timeline begins on the agreed kickoff date, scheduled after contract signing and the deposit.

I take one active sprint at a time. Kickoffs run on the fixed dates listed at the top of this page, and the paid deposit locks yours.

Client access, decision-maker availability, and timely feedback are required for the 10-business-day timeline.

### This is for you if…

- You run or lead product at a B2B SaaS company

- You know AI should be part of your product but do not want vague experimentation

- You want one useful AI workflow, not a giant AI transformation

- Your team can provide access to relevant product, data, or codebase context

- You can make decisions quickly during the sprint

- You want product judgment and execution, not just code

### This is not for you if…

- You want to "add AI" without a real user workflow

- You need a full enterprise AI transformation

- Your data is inaccessible or not ready

- Your team cannot provide access or feedback during the sprint

- You want a general chatbot without a clear product use case

- You need guaranteed production deployment regardless of infrastructure constraints

### FAQ

#### What is a 10-day FDE Sprint?

A 10-business-day engagement to ship one narrow AI workflow into a B2B SaaS product. Scoping on Day 1, design on Days 2 to 3, prototype by Day 5, implementation on Days 6 to 9, handoff on Day 10. Fixed scope, fixed price. Deliverables include the workflow code committed to your repo, an output quality rubric, a workflow playbook, a Loom walkthrough, and a 30-day post-Sprint roadmap.

#### How long does it take to ship an AI feature in a SaaS product?

Ten business days for one narrow workflow, if codebase access and sample data are ready on Day 1. Day 1 scopes it, Days 2 and 3 design it, a working prototype runs on your data by Day 5, and Day 10 is handoff. A broader AI feature takes longer; the Sprint ships its first narrow slice.

#### How do I know if my AI feature idea is feasible?

It's feasible in ten days if one person runs it, its data sits in one system you can export, it fits your existing APIs, and a person reviews the output before anything leaves. The [Workflow Scorecard](https://ghanemzadeh.com/scorecard/) checks this in two minutes across eight dimensions and four readiness checks.

#### Who is this for?

Founder-led B2B SaaS companies with 5 to 50 employees, post-product-market-fit, with paying customers, real data inside their product, and pressure to ship AI features. Not for indie hackers, solopreneurs, or enterprises with formal procurement.

#### What does it cost?

$5,000 for Sprints kicking off through Tuesday November 17, and $7,500 from the Tuesday December 1 kickoff. Half on signing, half on Day 10. The optional Discovery Day is $500, credited to the Sprint.

#### How do I justify the cost to my co-founder or board?

With your own numbers. For an internal workflow: the hours a week the work takes today, times the loaded hourly cost, times 52. Divide the Sprint price by the weekly saving and you have the payback period. In the worked example, a support summarizer that saves 20 hours a week pays back in under ten weeks. For a customer-facing feature, use the deal or retention metric it moves. Either way, the number goes into the value line of the Brief draft you get after the Scoping Call, so the case is written down before you pay anything.

#### Why is the Scoping Call free?

Some founders who take it ask me to run the Sprint. That's how I earn. The rest keep the scope.

#### What happens if you can't deliver?

A full refund, at either of two checkpoints. No working prototype on your data by Day 5? Stop the Sprint, full refund. The workflow in your signed Brief isn't running to its acceptance criteria by Day 10? Full refund.

#### Do you have case studies?

Not yet. This is a new offer. What you can see is the same kind of workflow built into Vectig, my own product, with numbers from my own test runs. That's why the price is $5,000 through November and why the guarantee is a full refund.

#### Why pay you instead of using your own engineers?

Speed, mostly: 10 days instead of six weeks of internal roadmap displacement, when pulling two engineers off the roadmap costs roughly $30K in salary before the opportunity cost. The rest is judgment. Knowing which workflow to ship first is harder than building it, and a fixed price on a fixed timeline keeps the scope honest.

#### We tried building an AI feature and it stalled. Why would this be different?

Most AI features stall in the same three places: a demo that worked on five examples, no agreement on what good output looks like, and nobody owning the last stretch to production. The Sprint is built against all three. Day 1 ends with a signed Brief that names one user, one input, one output, and the acceptance criteria. Day 5 is a working prototype on your real data, or you stop and get your money back. Days 6 to 9 are the edge cases, error states, and prompt tuning that demos skip, scored against the output rubric.

#### How is this different from an AI consulting firm?

This Sprint ships a working AI workflow into your codebase by Day 10, where AI consulting firms deliver decks and roadmaps. The category is "Forward Deployed AI Engineering": the same shape of work OpenAI's Deployment Company sells to large organizations and Anthropic's new services company to mid-sized ones, at a different price point.

#### Why hire an independent FDE instead of a model vendor's deployment team?

A vendor's forward deployed engineers work for the vendor, so the natural outcome is more of that vendor's platform and more spend on it. An independent FDE picks the model per workflow, keeps prompts and model settings in a config file your team controls, and can switch models when a better or cheaper one ships. Vendor teams also start at enterprise minimums; the FDE Sprint is sized for a 5 to 50 person company.

#### Is the FDE Sprint FDE as a service?

Yes, in fixed-scope form. Most FDE-as-a-service providers sell an engineer's time: by the hour through a talent marketplace, or by the month from a consultancy, where published prices run about $15,000 to $40,000 a month. The Sprint sells one shipped workflow instead: a fixed price, ten business days, and a full refund if it doesn't run. The [FDE-as-a-service market map](https://ghanemzadeh.com/fde-as-a-service/) compares 33 providers and every price they publish.

#### Should I hire a fractional forward deployed engineer instead?

A fractional FDE works part-time on a retainer, often two fixed days a week for three months or more, with scope that moves as the work goes. That fits ongoing AI work once you know what to build. If your first workflow hasn't shipped yet, a Sprint settles what to build and proves it on your data in ten days. A fractional engagement or a hire can follow, with a working example to point at.

#### What does it cost to hire a forward deployed engineer for a project?

In October 2026, published prices for outside FDE work run from $29 an hour for Asia-based contractors to $50 to $99 an hour from European firms. One provider's rate card puts a mid-level US contractor at $119 to $185 an hour. Embedded engineers from consultancies cost about $15,000 to $40,000 a month, and a senior builder through A.Team about $25,000 a month. The FDE Sprint is a fixed $5,000 for one workflow. The [FDE cost calculator](https://ghanemzadeh.com/fde-cost-calculator/) compares a hire, a contractor, and a Sprint.

#### What kinds of AI workflows do you build?

Narrow workflows with one input, one output, and one user: investor update assistants, runway scenario explainers, customer summary generators, support ticket summarizers, report generators, and onboarding assistants. The common shape: narrow input, narrow output, single user, measurable improvement, human-in-the-loop review. Thirty more examples, by team, are in [AI use cases for B2B SaaS](https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-workflows-for-saas/).

#### Do you build AI agents?

Yes, when the workflow needs one: when the model has to call tools, look things up in your systems, or take several steps to produce its output. Many Sprint workflows reach your systems through MCP servers for exactly that. What I don't build in a first Sprint is an agent that acts on customers without a person approving it. Every v1 keeps a human in the loop, and autonomy comes later, when your team decides it's earned.

#### What if our data isn't ready?

Then a Sprint isn't the right starting point yet. The scorecard usually flags it in two minutes, and the Scoping Call will say so explicitly and recommend what to do first.

#### Do you handle compliance, security, GDPR, SOC 2?

No. Those are explicitly out of scope. The Sprint can produce a workflow that's ready to deploy through your existing compliance posture, but the compliance review itself is your team's work.

#### What stack do you work in?

Whatever you already use. The Sprint integrates with your existing product, your existing data sources (Stripe, HubSpot, Linear, Slack, Notion, Intercom, Zendesk, your CRM, your admin), and your existing AI provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI). The Sprint is too short to introduce new infrastructure.

#### What do you need from us?

Read-only codebase access, sample data, and one decision-maker who answers within a business day. About five hours of the founder's time across the ten days, most of it on Day 1.

#### Can you guarantee production deployment?

No. Production deployment depends on access, infrastructure, and third-party dependencies that aren't fully under our control. If production release is blocked, the deliverable is a staging deployment or a production-ready pull request your team can merge.

#### What happens after Day 10?

Your team runs the workflow. The rubric and playbook are built so they can maintain it without me, and most teams do. If you want a second workflow, book another Sprint within 6 months of handoff and it runs at the price you paid for the first. There's no retainer to keep the first one running.

### Terms used on this page

**Forward Deployed Engineer**

An engineer who embeds inside a customer's team and ships inside their codebase, rather than delivering an external dashboard or report. Originally Palantir's model; OpenAI and Anthropic both built deployment teams around it in 2026.

**FDE Sprint**

This offer. FDE stands for forward deployed engineer. 10 business days, one narrow AI workflow, fixed scope, fixed price.

**Workflow**

A specific process a user runs with clear inputs and outputs, producing a measurable improvement. The unit of work shipped in a Sprint. Not a "feature."

**Sprint Brief**

The one-to-two-page document written on Day 1 of a Sprint that defines scope, success criteria, the value line, deliverables, and explicit out-of-scope items. Part of the contract.

**Output Quality Rubric**

A 1 to 5 scoring checklist tuned to a specific workflow, used to evaluate generated outputs consistently after handoff.

**MCP**

Model Context Protocol, the standard for letting AI models talk to external systems. Many Sprint workflows integrate with customer systems via MCP servers.

Full definitions for these and more terms are in the [Forward Deployed AI Engineering glossary](https://ghanemzadeh.com/glossary/).

# AI Use Cases for B2B SaaS: 30 Workflows to Ship First

URL: https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-workflows-for-saas/

[FDE Sprint](https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-feature-sprint/)

## AI use cases for B2B SaaS: 30 workflows, and which one to ship first

The AI use cases that actually ship in a B2B SaaS company are narrow: one user, one input, one output, and a person who checks the result. Below are 30 of them, grouped by team. Each is written as the one-sentence scope that opens a Sprint Brief, with the data it needs, its risk tier, and whether it fits a first ten-day Sprint. Most first workflows should be internal, and low or medium risk.

By [Nasser Ghanemzadeh](https://ghanemzadeh.com/). Last updated October 2026.

### How to read the list

Every entry follows the same sentence: *for* a user, *when* something happens, the workflow *will* do one thing and *produce* one output, *so that* something improves. If you can't fill those five slots for your idea, it isn't scoped yet.

- Low risk Internal only. The people who review the output are the people who asked for it.

- Medium risk Touches customer data, financial data, or appears in your product, with a person reviewing before anything leaves.

- High risk Legal, compliance, payments, or autonomous actions toward customers. Not a first Sprint.

Jump to: Support · Sales · Customer success · Finance and operations · Product and onboarding · Engineering and internal reporting

### Support

Support teams read a lot of text and write a lot of near-identical replies. Both are good first workflows, because an agent already reviews every reply before it goes out.

- **Ticket thread summarizer**For a support agent, when a ticket thread runs past ten messages, the workflow will read it and write the issue, what has been tried, and a suggested next step into the ticket sidebar, so that the agent can reply without rereading the history. Medium risk · Data: Zendesk, Intercom, or Help Scout · First Sprint: Yes

- **Reply drafter from your help center**For a support agent, when a how-to question arrives, the workflow will find the matching help-center articles and draft a reply that links to them, so that common questions are answered in one pass. Medium risk · Data: Help center articles and past solved tickets · First Sprint: Yes

- **Ticket triage**For the support lead, when a ticket is created, the workflow will suggest a category, product area, and urgency, so that the queue is sorted before anyone opens it. Medium risk · Data: Helpdesk tickets and your tag history · First Sprint: Yes

- **Bug report writer**For the engineer on call, when support escalates a ticket, the workflow will turn the thread into a bug report with steps to reproduce, the account, and links to logs, so that engineering gets a usable issue the first time. Medium risk · Data: Helpdesk plus Linear, Jira, or GitHub Issues · First Sprint: Yes

- **Weekly support themes**For the product lead, at the end of each week, the workflow will group the week's tickets into themes with counts and example quotes, so that product decisions start from what customers actually report. Medium risk · Data: Helpdesk export · First Sprint: Yes

### Sales

Sales workflows pay off fast because the inputs already exist as call transcripts and CRM records. Keep the rep as the one who sends anything to a prospect.

- **Call notes to CRM**For an account executive, when a sales call transcript is ready, the workflow will write the summary, next steps, and qualification fields into the CRM deal, so that the CRM stays current without after-call admin. Medium risk · Data: Gong, Fathom, or Zoom transcripts, and HubSpot or Salesforce · First Sprint: Yes

- **Account research brief**For an account executive, when a first call is booked, the workflow will compile the account's website, CRM history, and product signups into a one-page brief, so that the call starts informed. Medium risk · Data: CRM, signup data, and the prospect's public website · First Sprint: Yes

- **Follow-up email drafter**For an account executive, after a call, the workflow will draft the follow-up email from the transcript and the deal stage, so that follow-ups go out the same day. Medium risk · Data: Call transcripts and CRM deal stage · First Sprint: Yes

- **Inbound lead qualifier**For the sales team, when a demo request comes in, the workflow will score it against your ideal customer profile and write the reason for the score, so that reps call the best-fit accounts first. Medium risk · Data: Signup or demo form, enrichment data, and CRM · First Sprint: Yes

- **Security questionnaire drafter**For the founder, when a prospect sends a security questionnaire, the workflow will draft answers from past questionnaires and your policy documents and flag every answer it can't support, so that a two-day task becomes a review. High risk · Data: Past questionnaires and security policies · First Sprint: No. Compliance answers carry contract risk, so ship a lower-risk workflow first.

### Customer success

Customer success runs on context scattered across the CRM, the helpdesk, and product analytics. Pulling it into one place before a call is the most common first win.

- **Pre-renewal account summary**For the account owner, two weeks before a renewal, the workflow will pull the account's CRM notes, usage, and open tickets and write a one-page summary into the CRM record, so that the renewal call starts from the full picture. Medium risk · Data: CRM, product analytics, and helpdesk · First Sprint: Yes

- **At-risk account explainer**For a customer success manager, each week, the workflow will read the usage drops, tickets, and survey comments of accounts already flagged as at risk and write why each one looks at risk, so that outreach starts with a reason. Medium risk · Data: Product analytics, helpdesk, and CRM · First Sprint: Narrow slice first: explain accounts your existing rules already flag. Predicting churn is a separate project.

- **Quarterly review drafter**For a customer success manager, before a quarterly business review, the workflow will turn the account's usage numbers and the quarter's tickets into a draft review outline, so that prep starts from a draft. Medium risk · Data: Product analytics, helpdesk, and CRM · First Sprint: Yes

- **Feature request clustering**For the product lead, each month, the workflow will group feature requests from CRM notes, tickets, and call transcripts into themes linked to the accounts that asked, so that roadmap calls can weigh requests by revenue. Medium risk · Data: CRM, helpdesk, and call transcripts · First Sprint: Narrow slice first: start with one source, usually the helpdesk.

- **Setup check-in drafter**For a customer success manager, when a new account stalls on a setup step, the workflow will draft a check-in email based on what the account has set up so far, so that the nudge is specific instead of generic. Medium risk · Data: Product events and CRM · First Sprint: Yes

### Finance and operations

In a 5 to 50 person company, finance work usually lands on a founder. These workflows draft and explain; a person still checks every number.

- **Investor update assistant**For the founder, when the month's metrics and a few sentences of context are added, the workflow will draft the investor update covering metrics, risks, and asks, so that updates go out every month, on time. Medium risk · Data: Stripe, your finance sheet, or your accounting system · First Sprint: Yes

- **Runway scenario explainer**For the founder, when a change is proposed (a hire, a price change, a churn assumption), the workflow will run it against current burn and revenue and write what it does to runway in plain language, so that the decision is made with the number in front of everyone. Medium risk · Data: Your finance model or accounting system · First Sprint: Yes

- **Expense categorizer**For whoever does the books, when card and bank transactions sync, the workflow will suggest a category and a note for each and flag anything unusual, so that month-end close starts from a reviewed list. Medium risk · Data: Bank feed and Xero or QuickBooks · First Sprint: Yes

- **Software spend review**For the operations lead, each month, the workflow will read card transactions and flag duplicate tools, renewals coming up, and subscriptions nobody has logged into, so that unused spend gets cancelled before it renews. Medium risk · Data: Card or bank export and your accounting system · First Sprint: Yes

- **Contract terms extractor**For the founder, when a customer contract is signed, the workflow will pull the term, price, renewal date, notice period, and special terms into the CRM, so that renewals and obligations don't live only in PDFs. High risk · Data: Signed contracts and CRM · First Sprint: Not as stated. Renewal dates and prices only, checked by a person, is a medium-risk first Sprint.

### Product and onboarding

These run inside your product, in front of your customers. They are the ones that show up in sales demos, and they need the clearest acceptance criteria.

- **Onboarding assistant**For a new user, when they finish signing up, the workflow will use their setup data to suggest the next step in your product's first key workflow, inside the app, so that more new accounts reach first value. Medium risk · Data: Your product database and event data · First Sprint: Yes

- **Plain-language filters**For a user of your product, when they type a question such as "accounts over $10K with no login this month", the workflow will turn it into a filter on their data and show the result, so that they get answers without building a report. Medium risk · Data: Your product database or API · First Sprint: Narrow slice first: one object, read-only queries.

- **Report summary**For a user of your product, when they open a dashboard, the workflow will write three sentences on what changed since last period and what it likely means, so that the numbers arrive with a reading. Medium risk · Data: Your product's reporting data · First Sprint: Yes

- **Import mapper**For a new customer, when they upload a CSV, the workflow will suggest how their columns map to your fields and flag the rows that won't import, so that onboarding doesn't stall on a spreadsheet. Medium risk · Data: The customer's file and your schema · First Sprint: Yes

- **First-draft generator**For a user of your product, when they create a new record of your product's core type (a proposal, a job post, a campaign), the workflow will draft it from their past ones and a short prompt, so that they start from a draft instead of a blank page. Medium risk · Data: The user's past records in your product · First Sprint: Yes

### Engineering and internal reporting

Internal workflows are the safest first Sprint: no customer sees the output, and the people reviewing it are the people who asked for it.

- **Weekly report generator**For the founder or team lead, every Monday, the workflow will turn last week's product data and notes into the weekly internal report in your template, so that the report writes itself and someone only edits it. Low risk · Data: Product analytics and your notes · First Sprint: Yes

- **Release notes writer**For the product manager, when a release is tagged, the workflow will read the merged pull requests and tickets and draft customer-facing release notes and an internal changelog, so that every release gets announced. Low risk · Data: GitHub and Linear or Jira · First Sprint: Yes

- **Meeting notes to tasks**For a team lead, after an internal meeting, the workflow will turn the transcript into decisions and tasks with owners in your project tool, so that action items don't get lost. Low risk · Data: Meeting transcripts and Linear, Asana, or Jira · First Sprint: Yes

- **Internal docs answers**For a new hire, when they ask a question in Slack, the workflow will answer from your internal docs with links, and say when it doesn't know, so that onboarding questions stop interrupting senior people. Low risk · Data: Notion or Confluence, and Slack · First Sprint: Narrow slice first: one documentation space.

- **Error spike triage**For the engineer on call, when an error-rate alert fires, the workflow will group the errors, link them to recent deploys, and write a probable-cause summary, so that triage starts from a hypothesis. Low risk · Data: Sentry or your error tracker, and deploy history · First Sprint: Yes

### How to pick the first one

Pick the workflow that does well on four questions:

- It runs at least weekly, so the team feels the difference and you collect examples fast.

- Its data sits in one system you can export today.

- A person already reviews this kind of output, so a human check costs nothing new.

- You can say what a good output looks like, in a sentence, before anything is built.

Then put a number on it. For an internal workflow: the hours a week the work takes today, times the loaded hourly cost, times 52. For a feature in your product: the deal or retention metric it moves. The Sprint page shows [the worked example](https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-feature-sprint/#what-the-workflow-is-worth).

The [AI Workflow Scorecard](https://ghanemzadeh.com/scorecard/) runs your candidate through eight dimensions and four readiness checks in two minutes.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What are the best AI use cases for a B2B SaaS company?

The narrow ones: one user, one input, one output, and a person who checks the result. Support thread summaries, call notes written into the CRM, pre-renewal account summaries, release notes, and in-app report summaries all fit that shape. Start with a workflow that runs at least weekly and whose data sits in one system you can export.

#### Should the first AI feature be internal or customer-facing?

Usually internal. An internal workflow is reviewed by the people who asked for it, so mistakes are cheap and the team learns what good output looks like. Customer-facing features come next, once you have a rubric and an evaluation set from the first one.

#### How long does it take to build one of these?

Ten business days for one narrow workflow, if codebase access and sample data are ready on Day 1. That's the FDE Sprint: scoped on Day 1, a working prototype on your data by Day 5, in your repo by Day 10. Broader versions take longer; the Sprint ships the first narrow slice.

#### Should we start with an AI agent instead?

Start with a workflow that has a human check, then add agent behavior where the workflow needs it: calling tools, looking things up in your systems, taking several steps. An agent that acts on customers without a person approving it is a poor first project, because nobody has measured yet what good output looks like.

# The Best Forward Deployed Engineer Books & Resources (2026)

URL: https://ghanemzadeh.com/best-forward-deployed-engineer-books/

[Forward Deployed Engineer](https://ghanemzadeh.com/forward-deployed-ai-engineer/)

## The best Forward Deployed Engineer books & resources (2026)

The Forward Deployed Engineer role now has a shelf of its own: six books written about it, all from 2026, from a free 93-page PDF to a 746-page practitioner manual. A useful reading list pairs one of them with the best books on the skills the role is made of: AI engineering, data systems, product discovery, and the customer room. One of the six is mine, so it is listed first and disclosed; the comparison below says when another one is the better pick.

By [Nasser Ghanemzadeh](https://ghanemzadeh.com/). Last updated October 2026.

### Books written about the FDE role

#### 1. Forward Deployed AI Engineering, by Nasser Ghanemzadeh

The working guide to the role itself: what an FDE is, where the model came from, how the work is practiced phase by phase, and how to break in. 304 pages across five parts and 20 chapters, with a workbook and annotated references at the back; first edition May 2026, updated August 2026, in paperback and on Kindle. It is strongest on the whole arc of an engagement and on the path into the job. Full disclosure: I wrote this one.

[Read about the book](https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/forward-deployed-ai-engineering/), including the full structure and sample chapters.

#### 2. The Forward Deployed Engineer, by Paden Gayle (O'Reilly)

The O'Reilly entry, still in early release: the table of contents is marked not yet final, and O'Reilly lists the finished book for December 2027 at 350 pages. Gayle works as a forward deployed AI engineer at Notion, after engineering roles at Google and Bloomberg, and the book reads from inside the enterprise engagement, opening with "The Founder Inside Someone Else's Company." Pick it if you have O'Reilly access and want the view of someone doing the job now. [O'Reilly](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/the-forward-deployed/0642572416485/).

#### 3. FDE: Forward Deployed Engineer, by Srinivas Bommena

The largest book on the shelf: *The Practitioner Playbook for Shipping Enterprise AI*, 746 pages on Kindle in its third edition, also sold as *Shipping Enterprise AI: The Forward Deployed Engineer's Playbook*. The third edition goes deepest of the six into agent engineering: bounded coding-agent delegation, sub-agent and skill boundaries, retries and recovery, and tool and API integration. Pick it if you already do the work and want an engineering reference rather than an introduction. [Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H2D6RV8L).

#### 4. The Field Deployed Engineer's Handbook, by Daniel Vaughan (Leanpub)

*Production AI in the Real World*, written in public on Leanpub and 90% complete as of October 2026. Vaughan, a UK-based software architect specialising in agentic AI, follows the full engagement from the first customer conversation to production, adoption, and handover, and keeps the advice independent of any one vendor or platform. It assumes professional engineering experience. Pick it if you want a platform-neutral handbook and don't mind reading a book before it is finished. [Leanpub](https://leanpub.com/fde-handbook).

#### 5. How to Be a Forward Deployed Engineer, by Jason Mann

*The Complete Playbook for Enterprise Deployments, Customer Success, and Technical Excellence*: an independently published paperback from June 2026, 230 pages. It is pitched at engineers moving into the role, with breaking in, scoping, debugging in production, talking to executives, and measuring business value. Pick it for a compact career field guide. [Books-A-Million](https://www.booksamillion.com/p/How-Be-Forward-Deployed-Engineer/Jason-Mann/9798181160132).

#### 6. The Forward-Deployed Engineer, by Gennaro Cuofano

*A Playbook for the AI Era's Field Role*, a free 93-page book with 35 plates from The Business Engineer, first edition August 2026, delivered as a PDF in exchange for an email address. It is more business analysis than engineering: the "last mile" between what a model can do and what an enterprise will let it do, a four-gate test for picking the first problem, and a handover run as an acceptance test. Pick it if you are deciding whether to use FDEs, not how to be one. [The Business Engineer](https://fourweekmba.com/fde-playbook-book/).

In Chinese, the writer Fan Bing (范冰), author of *Growth Hacker*, published *前线部署工程师* free on GitHub in July 2026; it documents 165 cases from Palantir, OpenAI, and Anthropic to China's first FDE teams, and has about 5,000 stars. [GitHub](https://github.com/xdash/FDE-the-Guidance-Book-of-Forward-Deployed-Engineer).

### The six, side by side

| Book | Format and status | Length | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Forward Deployed AI Engineering (Ghanemzadeh) | Paperback and Kindle, updated August 2026 | 304 pages | The whole engagement arc and the path into the role |
| The Forward Deployed Engineer (Gayle) | O'Reilly early release; final edition listed for December 2027 | 350 pages (listed) | The enterprise view from a practising FDE |
| FDE: Forward Deployed Engineer (Bommena) | Kindle, third edition | 746 pages | Agent engineering in depth, for people already in the job |
| The Field Deployed Engineer's Handbook (Vaughan) | Leanpub, 90% complete | In progress | A platform-neutral handbook from discovery to handover |
| How to Be a Forward Deployed Engineer (Mann) | Paperback, June 2026 | 230 pages | A compact career field guide |
| The Forward-Deployed Engineer (Cuofano) | Free PDF for an email, August 2026 | 93 pages | Buyers and leaders deciding whether to use FDEs |

Details as listed by each publisher or store on October 12, 2026.

### Books on the skills the role is made of

No FDE book replaces the fundamentals. These four are the ones I would pair with whichever of the six you choose.

#### 1. AI Engineering, by Chip Huyen

The technical complement. Huyen covers building applications with foundation models: evaluation, prompt engineering, retrieval, finetuning decisions, and inference. If the FDE books are about the job, this is the deepest treatment of the engineering underneath it. For readers who want the model-layer fundamentals before their first engagement.

#### 2. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, by Martin Kleppmann and Chris Riccomini

The systems substrate of enterprise integration work. Most FDE engagements are won or lost on data plumbing, and this is the standard text on the storage, replication, and pipeline machinery inside every enterprise stack you will integrate with. Read it slowly. It pays off for years.

#### 3. Inspired, 2nd edition, by Marty Cagan

The product-discovery half of the craft. An FDE decides what to build under pressure, in front of the customer, and Cagan's book is the standard text on discovering what is worth building before you build it. Written for product teams, but the discovery discipline maps directly onto scoping an engagement.

#### 4. Impro, by Keith Johnstone

The odd one out, deliberately. Johnstone's book on improvisational theatre appears on Palantir's FDE onboarding reading list because customer-room work is improvisation: status, listening, and responding honestly to what is actually happening. It teaches the temperament of the work rather than the technique.

Running a B2B SaaS company? The method in this book is also a service, the FDE Sprint: one AI workflow shipped into your product in ten business days.

[Score your workflow (2 min)](https://ghanemzadeh.com/scorecard/) · [See the Sprint](https://ghanemzadeh.com/ai-feature-sprint/)

### Essential essays and talks (free)

- [How Palantir built the ultimate founder factory](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/inside-palantir-nabeel-qureshi). Nabeel Qureshi with Lenny Rachitsky, Lenny's Newsletter, May 2025. Reflections on nearly eight years as a Palantir forward deployed engineer, and why the role keeps producing founders.

- [The FDE Playbook for AI Startups](https://www.ycombinator.com/library/Mt-the-fde-playbook-for-ai-startups-with-bob-mcgrew). Bob McGrew on Y Combinator's Lightcone podcast, September 2025. The person who helped pioneer the model at Palantir, and later led research at OpenAI, explains why it is at the heart of the AI boom.

- [The Sales Strategy Conquering the AI Market](https://tomtunguz.com/fde-cs/). Tomasz Tunguz, July 2025. The go-to-market economics of forward deployed engineering, from the investor side.

- [Forward Deployed Engineering 101](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KwhgfwOSToQ). Kevin Bai at the AI Engineer World's Fair, June 2026. A 17-minute framework for when FDE is necessary and how to structure it, from someone who did the work at Palantir, Rippling, and Anthropic.

- [Software Is Changing (Again)](https://www.ycombinator.com/library/MW-andrej-karpathy-software-is-changing-again). Andrej Karpathy at YC's AI Startup School, June 2025. The wider shift the FDE role sits inside: LLMs as a new kind of computer, programmed in English.

### Where to start

If you are deciding whether the role is for you, start with the [explainer on what a Forward Deployed Engineer is](https://ghanemzadeh.com/forward-deployed-ai-engineer/), then the Qureshi and McGrew conversations. If you have decided and want the map, start with [Forward Deployed AI Engineering](https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/forward-deployed-ai-engineering/) and follow the path in [how to become an FDE](https://ghanemzadeh.com/how-to-become-a-forward-deployed-ai-engineer/). If you are already in the role, Bommena's third edition and Vaughan's handbook go deeper on the engineering. If you are buying FDE work rather than doing it, start with Cuofano's free book, then [the three ways a startup can get one](https://ghanemzadeh.com/forward-deployed-engineer-for-startups/).

# The Founder Mode Book: From HP to NVIDIA | Nasser Ghanemzadeh

URL: https://ghanemzadeh.com/book/

**Brian Chesky just reopened the AI Founder Mode conversation for the AI Era.** This book turns the idea into an operating lens.

A practical book on how founders stay close to product, people, judgment, and execution as companies scale.

## Founder Mode

*How the Great Companies Are Actually Built*

In 2024, Paul Graham named "Founder Mode" after Brian Chesky's talk at a YC alumni dinner. The practice is older than the name. HP, Disney, Apple, Pixar, Amazon, NVIDIA, and Costco built their best work this way. This book traces how, and is honest about the costs.

Sign up to be notified when the book ships. The first two chapters are yours to read now.

You'll also get the newsletter. One email a week, easy unsubscribe.

### Why this book, now

Founder Mode is back in the conversation because Brian Chesky is again explaining how great founders operate differently. But the idea is still easy to misunderstand. Founder Mode is not micromanagement. It is not founder ego. It is calibrated involvement: staying close to the decisions, standards, customers, products, and people that shape the company.

02 · What's inside

### Four parts

**Foundations** lays out what Founder Mode actually is, separating the practice from the personality around it.

**Practices** is the operating manual. The small group of trusted operators. The meetings the founder still runs personally. The decisions the founder still owns. The handoffs that have to happen anyway.

**Anchors** is the case-study core. Eight companies, eight chapters, and the specific moves that made each one work.

**Returns, Costs, Coda** is the part most books skip. Founder Mode works, and it costs the founder things. The book is honest about both.

03 · Anchor chapters

### Eight companies, eight chapters

#### HP

Bill and Dave still walking the lab decades after founding, and the practice that institutionalized it.

#### Walt Disney

The *Snow White* production and a $1.5M bet on feature animation when nobody believed it would work.

#### PayPal

The small group, the relentless iteration, and the alumni network it produced.

#### Apple

Jobs in the Newton era. The products that almost shipped, the ones that did, and what he refused to delegate.

#### Pixar

Ed Catmull's Brain Trust as a structured, durable form of involvement.

#### Amazon

Bezos's Day 1 doctrine and the six-page memos that enforced it.

#### NVIDIA

Jensen Huang at Denny's, then thirty years of the same direct-report meetings.

#### Costco

The buying-club discipline that survived Sinegal's retirement.

# Books Like The Daily Stoic for Founders and Investors

URL: https://ghanemzadeh.com/books-like-the-daily-stoic/

[Books](https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/)

## Books like The Daily Stoic for founders, investors, and managers

The Daily Stoic made the one-page-a-day book popular again. If you decide for a living, six more in the same format are worth a year: The Daily Laws for power and people, The Daily Drucker for management, The Daily Pressfield for doing the work, Limitless Daily for focus and learning, Tolstoy's A Calendar of Wisdom for the oldest version of the form, and Daily Wisdom for mental models, misjudgment, and money.

By [Nasser Ghanemzadeh](https://ghanemzadeh.com/). Last updated October 2026.

### The seven books

#### 1. The Daily Stoic, by Ryan Holiday and Stephen Hanselman (2016)

The book that brought the form back. Each day pairs a short passage from Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, Epictetus, or another Stoic with a page of commentary on how to use it now. The subject is the inner game: what you control, what you don't, and how to stay steady when the second category misbehaves. It is the right first daily book for almost anyone, which is also its limit. It says little about money, markets, or running a company.

#### 2. The Daily Laws, by Robert Greene (2021)

Greene distilled his books on power, seduction, mastery, strategy, and human nature into a page a day, with each month built around one theme. Read it to understand people: why the colleague resists, why the negotiation stalls, why the board behaves as it does. It is sharper on reading others than on judging yourself.

#### 3. The Daily Drucker, by Peter F. Drucker with Joseph A. Maciariello (2004)

366 readings drawn from Drucker's work on management, each ending with an action point. Time, decisions, innovation, the effective executive. The examples are from the twentieth century; the principles have aged better than most management writing since. The best daily book for anyone who runs a team.

#### 4. A Calendar of Wisdom, by Leo Tolstoy

The oldest book here. Tolstoy spent his last years collecting thoughts from philosophers, prophets, and writers, grouped by a topic for each day, with his own reflections added. Peter Sekirin's English translation appeared in 1997. It is a book about how to live rather than how to decide, and it is the reminder that the daily form is a practice, not a modern productivity trick.

#### 5. The Daily Pressfield, by Steven Pressfield (2023)

365 days, plus a bonus week, from the author of *The War of Art*. Each day opens with a passage from Pressfield's work, among them *The War of Art*, *Gates of Fire*, and his Writing Wednesdays blog, followed by his commentary on it. Victor Juhasz drew one illustration for each week. The book follows a project rather than the calendar: you open to page one when you start a book, an album, or a company, and it walks with you to the finish. The subject is Resistance, Pressfield's name for the force that keeps you from starting the work that matters, and the professional habits that beat it. It is written for writers and artists first, but anyone building a company from nothing will recognize the enemy. It is better on showing up to do the work than on judging which work to do.

#### 6. Limitless Daily, by Jim Kwik (2026)

From the author of *Limitless*, published in September 2026. Kwik turns his brain training into 366 short morning pages on the instrument you decide with, across five areas: mindset, focus, flow, learning, and habits. Each page is one small idea, built to be read in a few minutes before the day starts. It is the most practical book on this list about attention and learning, and the least about money, markets, or managing people.

#### 7. Daily Wisdom, by Nasser Ghanemzadeh (2026)

366 one-page meditations for founders, investors, and managers, in the mental-model tradition of Charlie Munger and Peter Bevelin. Each page has three parts: a quotation checked against its primary source, an essay of about 250 words, and one question or action to carry into the day. The year is a course: the latticework of mental models in January, the psychology of misjudgment in February and March, then the mathematics of wisdom, money, the investor's temperament, the manager's craft, the founder's path, and a not-to-do list built from history's disasters. It is the one on this list written for decisions with money, runway, and other people's trust at stake. Full disclosure: I wrote this one.

[See every page title](https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/daily-wisdom/), all 366, with two days printed in full.

### Side by side

| Book | Subject | Each day | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The Daily Stoic | Stoic philosophy: control, emotion, character | A Stoic passage and a page of commentary | Anyone starting a daily practice |
| The Daily Laws | Power, strategy, and human nature | A page distilled from Greene's books, under a monthly theme | Reading people and organizations |
| The Daily Drucker | Management and effectiveness | A Drucker reading and an action point | Managers and executives |
| A Calendar of Wisdom | How to live | Collected thoughts on one topic, with Tolstoy's reflections | Life questions, not business ones |
| The Daily Pressfield | Resistance, creative work, and turning pro | A passage from Pressfield's work and his commentary on it, from a project's first day to its last | Founders and creators who keep putting off the real work |
| Limitless Daily | The brain: mindset, focus, learning, and habits | One short idea for the morning, from Kwik's brain training | Anyone who wants sharper focus and faster learning |
| Daily Wisdom | Mental models, misjudgment, and money | A verified quotation, a short essay, and one question or action | Founders, investors, and managers making costly decisions |

### How to choose

- **You want to stay steady under pressure.** Start with The Daily Stoic.

- **You keep misreading people.** The Daily Laws.

- **You run a team and want to run it better.** The Daily Drucker.

- **You know what to do and keep not doing it.** The Daily Pressfield.

- **Your bottleneck is focus or learning speed.** Limitless Daily.

- **You want the long view, beyond work.** A Calendar of Wisdom.

- **Your mistakes cost money: a hire, an investment, a partner, a burn rate.** Daily Wisdom. Start with [March 14, the pre-mortem](https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/daily-wisdom/#march-14), or [June 8, the Cobra effect](https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/daily-wisdom/#june-8).

Two daily books at once is one too many. Pick the one that matches the decisions in front of you this year, and keep a notebook next to it. The prompts only pay if the writing happens.

### Not daily, but the source

Two books sit underneath Daily Wisdom and much of this genre, and both reward a slow read after a year of pages. Peter Bevelin's *Seeking Wisdom: From Darwin to Munger* (2003) collects in one place what Darwin, Munger, Buffett, and a hundred scientists figured out about why we misjudge. *Poor Charlie's Almanack* gathers Charlie Munger's talks, including the one on the psychology of human misjudgment.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What is a good alternative to The Daily Stoic for business?

For management, The Daily Drucker: 366 readings from Peter Drucker, each with an action point. For power and human nature, Robert Greene's The Daily Laws. For decisions about money, hiring, and risk, Daily Wisdom, which applies Charlie Munger's mental models and the psychology of misjudgment to founders, investors, and managers, one page a day.

#### Is there a daily book about mental models?

Yes. Daily Wisdom for Founders, Investors, and Managers is 366 one-page meditations in the mental-model tradition of Charlie Munger and Peter Bevelin. Each page has a quotation checked against its primary source, an essay of about 250 words, and one question or action for the day.

#### Do you have to start a daily book on January 1?

No. Most books on this list are organized by date, so you can start on today's page and go round the year from there. The Daily Pressfield is the exception: it follows a project from start to finish rather than the calendar, so you open to page one when you begin something new. A second year through the same book reads differently from the first, because you are making different decisions.

Want to try a month first? [Daily Wisdom](https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/daily-wisdom/) is out on Kindle, in paperback, and in hardcover, and the November sampler, all thirty days of The Not-To-Do List with the decision journal, goes free to anyone who joins [the newsletter](https://ghanemzadeh.com/newsletter/).

# Daily Wisdom: 366 Meditations on Mental Models | Nasser Ghanemzadeh

URL: https://ghanemzadeh.com/books/daily-wisdom/

**Out now.** Daily Wisdom is on Kindle, in paperback, and in hardcover.

A year-long course in not fooling yourself: a verified quotation, a three-minute essay, and one question, for every day of the year.

## Daily Wisdom

*for Founders, Investors, and Managers: 366 Meditations on Mental Models, Misjudgment, and Money*

First edition · Kindle, paperback, and hardcover · 366 meditations · 399 pages in print

One bad hire costs a year. One bad acquisition costs a decade. One bad partner can cost you the company. Avoided mistakes compound like invested money, and almost nobody studies avoidance. The standard stupidities never go out of style: people overpaid for glamour stocks in 1720, in 1999, and in 2021, and founders ran out of cash in every decade on record. The names change. The errors are reruns. This book studies the reruns, one page a day, until you recognize them from the opening scene.

[Order Hardcover](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HHNYM63M/)
[Order Paperback](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HHNZJB9R/)
[Order on Kindle](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HHNNFY6M/)

Or read a whole month first: sign up and the November sampler, 54 pages, lands in your inbox.

You'll also get the newsletter. One email a week, easy unsubscribe.

02 · What it is

### One page a day

Start on today's date, or on January 1, or anywhere. The year is a circle; you will pass every page eventually.

Each page has three parts: a quotation, verified and attributed; a short essay; and a closing prompt, a question to sit with or a small action to take. The prompt is the point. Reading the page takes three minutes; the page only pays if the prompt survives into your day.

The months are themed, and later pages assume earlier ones the way a course assumes its prerequisites. Cross-references like "February 14" point back to the day where an idea was built. Ignore them on a first pass; they are for the second. At the back, Sources by Day lists where every quotation comes from, and Further Reading lists the books behind each month, in the order I would hand them to a friend.

Two habits multiply the book's value. Keep a notebook; many prompts ask you to write, and the writing is where the thinking happens. And reread. The same page reads differently in a bull market and a bear market, before a decision and after one.

03 · Who it's for

### Three readers

The pages rotate among three readers, because the three jobs share one underlying craft: making decisions under uncertainty, with other people's trust at stake. Most days speak to all three. All days speak to the person underneath the job.

- **The founder** watching runway. October is your month, but the base rates, the cash arithmetic, and the partner problems are spread across the year.

- **The investor** watching yourself. Temperament, not IQ, is the scarce input, and the barriers were never intellectual.

- **The manager** building a machine that runs without you. Design the incentives, deserve the trust, tell the truth fast, delegate to the edge, protect the standards.

And anyone who suspects the expensive mistakes are more avoidable than the successes are copyable.

04 · The year

### Twelve months, one argument

The content follows Peter Bevelin's map and the thinkers he drew on. The first half builds the frame and studies how the mind fails. The second half turns outward: money, investing, management, founding, and what all of it is for.

#### January · The Latticework

Knowledge only works when it hangs together. A fact you cannot connect is a fact you will forget. This month builds the frame the other eleven hang on.

#### February · The Machinery of Misjudgment

Your brain is legacy hardware. Bevelin, following Munger, cataloged twenty-eight psychological reasons we misjudge. One per day, with the leap day for what happens when several fire at once.

#### March · Guarding the Mind

February cataloged the bugs. March installs the patches: procedures, questions, and habits that catch the error before it ships. None of them are clever. All of them work because they don't depend on you being at your best.

#### April · The Mathematics of Wisdom

About ten ideas, held firmly: compounding, probability, expected value, regression, ruin. Most expensive errors are not calculation failures. They are failures to see that a calculation applies.

#### May · Lessons from Darwin

Markets are ecosystems with quarterly reporting. Variation and selection, niches and predators, signals and mimicry, extinction and adaptation. Where the analogy breaks, the book says so.

#### June · Systems and Second-Order Effects

A company is not a machine with levers. It is a system, and it answers every intervention with consequences you did not order. The fix is almost never "try harder."

#### July · The Psychology of Money

Money decisions are made in minds, by people with histories, fears, and neighbors. Morgan Housel's territory: why keeping wealth is a different skill from making it. Less math than April. More mirrors.

#### August · The Investor's Temperament

Everything you need to know about investing fits in a pamphlet, and the pamphlet has been public for ninety years. Almost nobody can follow it. The barriers are temperamental, not intellectual.

#### September · The Manager's Craft

Design the incentives, deserve the trust, tell the truth fast, delegate to the edge, protect the standards, build a machine that runs without you. None of it requires charisma. All of it requires spine.

#### October · The Founder's Path

Survival, focus, customers, cash, partners, pricing, and the long game, with the base rates in view and the romance left at the door. The failures cluster around a short list of preventable causes. This month is that list.

#### November · The Not-To-Do List

Munger's 1986 commencement trick: prescribe guaranteed misery and let the audience invert. The reliable roads to failure, then a week in Sherlock Holmes's company. Wisdom, this month insists, is mostly subtraction.

#### December · The Good Life

What is all this optimization for? The Stoics, whom Munger read and quoted; the virtues that outlast portfolios; the arithmetic of enough. Wisdom's last application is not a better decision. It is a life you would re-choose.

05 · Two pages from the book

### Two pages, unabridged

Every page in the book looks like these two. The first opens the year. The second opens November.

#### January 1 · Why Wisdom

> *"When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them."*

> CONFUCIUS, *Analects* (trans. James Legge)

Start with uncomfortable arithmetic. One bad hire costs a year. One bad acquisition costs a decade. One bad partner can cost you the company. Avoided mistakes compound like invested money. Almost nobody studies avoidance.

We study success stories instead. They flatter us. Failures instruct us, and we skip them.

Wisdom, as this book uses the word, is not brilliance. It is a working knowledge of how things fail, held firmly enough that you fail less often than the people around you. That is a real competitive advantage, because the standard stupidities never go out of style. People overpaid for glamour stocks in 1720, in 1999, and in 2021. Founders ran out of cash in every decade on record. The names change. The errors are reruns.

Confucius stated the entry fee twenty-five centuries ago. You will commit faults. The question is what happens next. Most people defend the fault, because admitting it stings. So they pay for the same lesson twice, then a third time, at rising prices. The second bill is rarely denominated in money alone. It comes in years, in partners, in the chance that does not come back.

This year, one page a day, we study the reruns until you recognize them from the opening scene.

**Ask yourself:** What mistake have I already paid for more than once? What would it take to actually abandon it?

#### November 1 · Consistently Not Stupid

> *"It is remarkable how much long-term advantage people like us have gotten by trying to be consistently not stupid, instead of trying to be very intelligent."*

> CHARLIE MUNGER

Munger is *not* claiming that brilliance is worthless, or that Berkshire won by accident. He is observing where the returns actually came from, and his answer is avoidance. Not the genius trades made, but the standard stupidities not committed: the leverage not taken, the manias not joined, the reputations not gambled. Buffett put it the same way in the 1989 letter, after twenty-five years of buying businesses. He and Munger had not learned to solve difficult business problems. They had learned to avoid them, by looking for one-foot hurdles to step over rather than seven-foot ones they might clear.

The arithmetic runs through this book. Errors are asymmetric. Losses require outsized gains to repair (April 20), and some end the game entirely; no accumulated brilliance survives one act of terminal stupidity. Errors are also more *predictable* than successes. Nobody can list next decade's winning ideas, but February's twenty-eight failure modes have been constant for centuries. Avoiding the known and recurring beats predicting the unknown, on reliability alone.

And the competition is thinner. The pursuit of brilliance is crowded with ambitious people bidding up the price of cleverness. The pursuit of non-stupidity is nearly deserted, because it is unglamorous, invisible when it works (January 29), and pays in disasters that never happened. Munger's folk saying completes the thought: it's the strong swimmers who drown. The confident, the brilliant, the credentialed swim out too far.

**Ask yourself:** Will this year's results improve more from one brilliant addition, or from deleting my two most repeatable stupidities? Name the two.
